findings.title: Truth and scale
findings.claim: The pericope makes the focus's 'best' speech accountable for truth and proportion as well as manner: it follows claims about God that are called grave and placed beneath divine exaltation.
findings.mechanism: The carrier is the focus's instruction to speak what is best. The independent trigger is 17:40's specific attribution about sons and female angels, followed by 17:43's statement that God is exalted above what they say. Their contact makes the standard answer not only how an utterance sounds but also what it asserts and how far its claim reaches.
findings.reader_payoff: Best speech becomes more than diplomacy: it must not enlarge an attribution beyond what the surrounding passage can bear.
findings.containment: The preceding claim is a specific theological attribution, not a universal example of every disagreement. The legacy HFT reads the magnitude language as speaker inflation, while 17:43 most directly describes God's exaltation; no speaker motive is settled, and the immediate focus can still emphasize manner.

epistemic.reason: All source coordinates agree with the supplied Arabic and root occurrences, and the focus join is exact. The interpretive extension from grave attribution to a truth-and-scale criterion is supported by the pericope but comes through a legacy_unbound HFT record.

findings.title: Faithful speech under blocked reception
findings.claim: The command assigns responsibility for the speaker's utterance without promising that good wording will persuade: the surrounding passage shows recitation met by barriers, turning away, and hostile private reframing.
findings.mechanism: The focus's q-w-l speech act is the carrier. The independent native context first says that Quranic reminders increase aversion, then depicts a barrier, covering, weighted hearing, withdrawal, and secret consultation. These conditions contact the instruction to say what is best and change it from a persuasion technique into fidelity under uncertain uptake.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can distinguish the quality of one's speech from control over another person's response.
findings.containment: The passage depicts particular resistant hearers and need not generalize to every audience. The HFT's 'verbal puncture' is retained as an analogy from the adjacency of speech and incitement; the text does not specify that Satan's incitement itself is a spoken jab. A live alternative is that the earlier barriers describe a special separation rather than a general communication model.

findings.containment: The 17:60 sequence describes divine warning and a resisting audience; transferring its result to human speech is exploratory. The tree/interweaving image is an attributed HFT analogy, and the passage does not establish a universal de-escalation rule or make all warnings unwise.

findings.title: Call, answer, and relation
findings.claim: As a contained analogy, the immediately preceding resurrection call and response makes renewed responsiveness imaginable in the focus: best speech can keep a damaged relation open where incitement tends to close it.
findings.mechanism: The 17:52 call and response are the contextual carriers. The independent focus trigger is the command to speak, the bond named by baynahum, and the incitement between people. The registered bond branch and the attributed call/answer mappings contact these elements, changing best speech from mere quarrel avoidance into a possible reopening of response.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see careful speech as preserving a route back into reply, not only suppressing conflict.
findings.containment: This transfers a resurrection call-and-response into an interpersonal analogy and does not collapse 17:53 into 17:52. The HFT identity is legacy_unbound. Its B-Y-N trace also names focus word 16, mubin ('clear'); only baynahum at word 10 carries the interpersonal bond used here.

epistemic.reason: The call and response coordinates match 17:52, and focus word 10 is the exact interpersonal bayn carrier. The cross-scene reanimation is a contained, surprising analogy from a legacy_unbound source.

findings.title: Speech in worshipful service
findings.claim: In the external overlay, the people addressed as 'my servants' can also be heard as a worshipping community, placing the speech command within their God-directed service and dependence.
findings.mechanism: The external carrier is 1:5's act of worship and request for help. The focus trigger is the address to 'my servants' together with the command that they speak. Their shared ʿ-b-d root creates a local contact: the external ayah supplies an active worship frame for the group receiving the speech instruction.
findings.reader_payoff: The overlay lets the ethical speech command appear as part of the life of a worshipping community, not only as social technique.
findings.containment: This remains an exploratory overlay: the external 'we' is not explicitly identified with the focus's servants, and 1:5 does not say that speaking well is itself worship. The root contact enriches the focus without replacing the native pericope reading.

epistemic.reason: The exact external form na'budu and focus form ʿibadi share the supplied root, and the focus branch has accepted lexical identity. The step from that contact to speech as conduct within worship is an analogical overlay; no separate trust label or HFT nomination is supplied.

friction_notes: All 19 focus-word joins resolve, and every HFT source word/root coordinate checked against the supplied surface. The reader identity remains legacy_unbound, so unresolved branch roles stay attributed rather than becoming independent lexical claims.
In 17:43 the elevation and grandeur most directly describe God's exaltation above the people's saying; the HFT link to speaker inflation remains an attributed possibility.
The 17:60 warning-to-transgression sequence describes divine warning to a resisting audience. Its transfer to human speech remains exploratory, including the tree/interweaving image.
The Fātiḥa 1:5 overlay has a direct root contact, but the packet does not establish that its first-person 'we' is identical to 17:53's 'my servants' or that the speech act itself is worship.
